opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing I'd say is that it's worth being honest about what a benchmark actually is. A benchmark is a proxy. It's a stand-in for something you care about, and the question is always how good that stand-in is for your particular problem. So when someone comes to me and says, "I'm trying to solve X in the real world, which benchmark should I use?", my instinct is to flip it around and ask, "What decision are you actually trying to make?"

Because in practice, benchmarks get used for very different purposes. Sometimes you're comparing models to pick one to deploy. Sometimes you're trying to track progress over time. Sometimes you're trying to understand failure modes or risks. And those purposes call for different kinds of measurement. A leaderboard number that's great for tracking broad progress in the field might tell you almost nothing about whether a model will work for, say, a clinical triage setting or a specific customer population.

So a few things I tend to look at. One is construct validity: does the thing the benchmark measures line up with the capability or behavior you care about? A lot of benchmarks are named after a broad concept, like "reasoning" or "safety", but when you look at the actual items, they're measuring something much narrower. That's not necessarily bad, but you need to know it.

Second is the distribution question. Is the data in the benchmark anything like the data your system will see? Different language, different user populations, different formats. Performance can shift quite a bit, and those shifts are often exactly where real-world harms show up.

Third, I think about contamination and saturation. If a benchmark has been around a long time, there's a decent chance models have effectively seen it, or that the field has overfit to it. High scores there may say more about familiarity than capability.

And then, honestly, a lot of the time the right answer is that no off-the-shelf benchmark is sufficient, and you need to build at least a small, targeted evaluation of your own. It doesn't have to be huge. Even a carefully constructed set of a few hundred examples that reflect your actual use case, with clear criteria for what "good" means, can be far more informative than a public leaderboard. The public benchmarks are a useful starting filter, but they shouldn't be the final word.

The broader point I'd make is that measurement is a scientific question in its own right. We should treat evaluation with the same rigor we treat modeling: thinking about uncertainty, about what our metrics really capture, and about whether the conclusions we draw are actually supported by the measurements we have.

r001.rationale: The response says public benchmarks are a useful starting point but may be insufficient, and recommends building a targeted evaluation that reflects the actual use case.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because benchmarks end up driving so much of what the field does, whether we intend it or not. The way I'd frame it is that a benchmark is really a proxy. It's a stand-in for the thing you actually care about, and the first question I'd ask is: how good is that proxy? What's the gap between doing well on this benchmark and actually solving the problem I have?

And that gap shows up in a few places. One is construct validity, to borrow the term from measurement science. Does the benchmark actually measure the capability you think it measures? A lot of benchmarks, when you look closely, end up measuring something adjacent. Maybe they're measuring memorization, or they're measuring a very narrow slice of a skill, or there are shortcuts in the data that let a model do well without doing the thing you care about. So I'd want to look at how the benchmark was constructed, what the data distribution looks like, and whether it's plausible that a model could score highly for the wrong reasons.

The second thing is distribution shift. Your real-world problem has a particular population, a particular set of inputs, a particular set of failure modes that matter to you. A public benchmark was built by someone else, for some other purpose, with some other population in mind. So even if the benchmark is well constructed, it may just not reflect your deployment setting. In a lot of cases, honestly, the right answer is that you should build your own evaluation, even if it's small, because a small evaluation that's actually representative of your setting is often more informative than a large one that isn't.

And then the third piece, which I think people underweight, is: what are the costs of errors? Benchmarks usually report a single number, accuracy or something like it, and that treats all mistakes as equivalent. In the real world they're almost never equivalent. If you're doing something in a healthcare setting, a false negative and a false positive have very different consequences. So I'd want to ask whether the metric encodes the costs that matter, and if it doesn't, whether I can at least disaggregate the results enough to see where the errors are landing and who's affected by them.

So the short version is, I treat benchmark selection as a measurement problem. You're trying to design or pick an instrument that gives you reliable, valid evidence about the question you actually have. And I'd be pretty skeptical of taking a leaderboard number at face value as evidence that something will work for you. It's a starting point, it's useful for comparing approaches at a coarse level, but it's rarely the thing that should make the final decision.

r001.rationale: The response weighs whether a public benchmark reflects the deployment setting and says a small, representative evaluation may be more informative, supporting a tailored benchmark when the existing one misses the problem’s specific issues.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to start with the problem you actually care about. What would success look like in the setting where this system is going to be used? And then work backward to ask whether the benchmark captures that.

There are at least two pieces to that question. One is the data: how well does it represent the people and situations you're going to encounter? The other is the metric: does improving that number actually mean you're doing a better job? You could have a very representative dataset and still choose a metric that hides the errors that matter most.

For example, if you're building a screening system, different kinds of mistakes may have very different consequences. Average accuracy isn't necessarily going to tell you what you need to know. You might care much more about missed cases, or performance for a particular group.

So I view a benchmark as a useful proxy. It lets us compare approaches and make progress, but we still have to establish that progress on the benchmark translates into progress on the real problem.

r001.rationale: The response says to check whether a benchmark’s data and metric reflect the real problem, but it does not ask whether to rely on an existing benchmark or invest in one tailored to that problem.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to start with the problem you actually care about. What decision is this system going to support? Who’s going to use it, and what does it mean for it to make a mistake? Those questions should drive the choice of benchmark and the metric you use to evaluate it.

A benchmark is necessarily a proxy. It gives you a particular dataset, a particular setting, and usually a fairly narrow definition of success. That can be very useful for comparing methods, but doing well on that benchmark doesn’t automatically tell you that you’ve solved the real-world problem.

So I’d ask how closely the benchmark reflects the deployment setting. Does it represent the people you expect to serve? Are the costs of different errors captured by the metric? And then, even if the average performance looks good, where does the system fail? You may need several evaluations to answer those questions, rather than a single number.

r001.rationale: The response says to check how closely a benchmark reflects deployment and suggests multiple evaluations, but it does not address whether to rely on an existing benchmark or invest in one tailored to the problem.
